sections.title: Start here: how to use this compendium and find your own method

items.title: Finding your method: how to experiment and track what works
items.lead: Treat finding a study method like a small experiment: try one change at a time, measure it honestly, and keep what works. The aim is a method that suits you…

items.title: Step 1: Start from a strong default
items.lead: Begin with retrieval and spacing (blank-page recall, flashcards, questions). Adjust from there rather than starting from scratch.

items.title: Step 2: Change one thing at a time
items.lead: For example, try concept maps instead of flashcards for one subject for one or two weeks.

items.title: Step 3: Give it enough time
items.lead: At least 5 sessions over 1 to 2 weeks. Every new method feels awkward at first.

items.title: Step 4: Rate every session
items.lead: How much did I recall the next day (1 to 5)? How much did I enjoy it? How focused was I? How much effort did it take?

items.title: Step 5: Use objective signals too
items.lead: Question-bank scores, how many gaps appear in blank-page recall, and how well topics hold up at the 7-day review.

items.title: Step 6: Decide: keep, tweak or drop
items.lead: Keep what scores well on both recall and enjoyment. Tweak what has good recall but feels boring. Drop what you enjoy but can't recall.

items.title: Step 7: Match methods to content
items.lead: One person may end up with flashcards for vocabulary, drawing for processes and worked problems for maths.

items.title: Step 8: Review monthly
items.lead: Methods that worked for one course or year may need to change for the next.

sections.title: How learning works: the principles behind every technique

items.title: Recognising is not remembering

items.title: Forgetting is part of the process
items.lead: Memory fades fast after first exposure (the forgetting curve). Each successful recall, especially when it takes some effort, makes the memory last longer.

items.title: Desirable difficulties

items.title: Understanding before memorising

items.title: Generation beats consumption
items.lead: Anything you produce yourself, such as an answer, a diagram, an explanation or a question, is remembered better than something you only read or watched.

items.title: Sleep consolidates memory
items.lead: What you study is stabilised during sleep, so an all-nighter costs the very memories it was meant to build.

items.title: Cramming vs deep learning

items.title: Interleaving
items.lead: Mix related topics or problem types in one session instead of blocking one topic at a time. It works best for topics that are easy to confuse.

items.title: Elaborative interrogation

items.title: Self-explanation

items.title: Feynman technique (explain it simply)
items.lead: Explain a topic in plain words as if to a 12-year-old. Where you get stuck or use jargon you can't unpack is where your understanding stops.

items.title: Learning by teaching
items.lead: Teach a classmate, a study group, or even an empty room. Preparing to teach also helps.

items.title: Dual coding
items.lead: Pair words with visuals: diagrams, flowcharts, timelines, sketches. Redraw them from memory.

items.title: Concrete examples
items.lead: Link every abstract idea to a concrete case, example or story.

items.title: Pretesting (errorful generation)
items.lead: Try questions on a topic before you study it. Getting them wrong primes you to notice the answers.

items.title: Successive relearning
items.lead: Keep retrieving each item until you get it right, then come back on later days and do it again.

items.title: A simple rule of thumb

items.title: Cornell notes

items.title: Question-based notes

items.title: Annotate the slides instead of rewriting them

items.title: Concept maps
items.lead: Boxes and labelled arrows (causes, inhibits, leads to, is an example of) show how ideas connect. Redraw them from memory a few days later.

items.title: Flowcharts and pathway sketches

items.title: Comparison tables

items.title: One-page summaries
items.lead: At the end of a topic, condense it onto one page. The act of choosing what matters is itself learning.

items.title: Longhand vs laptop

items.title: Pre-reading (priming)

items.title: Learning objectives as a checklist

items.title: Don't over-polish notes
items.lead: Beautiful, colour-coded notes can become a form of procrastination. Notes are only as good as how often you test yourself from them.

items.title: Which note format for which material?
items.lead: No single format is best. Match the format to the shape of the material: is it a set of questions, a web of relations, a sequence, a set of look-alikes, or a…

items.title: Anki and flashcards done well

items.title: Don't let cards replace understanding
items.lead: Learn the mechanism or the reasoning first, then card the details. A card you can't explain is a card you will forget.

items.title: Mnemonics and acronyms
items.lead: Useful for arbitrary lists like the cranial nerves, the order of the planets, the causes of a condition or the notes on a stave. Make them silly, vivid and…

items.title: Memory palace (method of loci)
items.lead: Place items along a route through a familiar place, such as your home. It works well for ordered lists.

items.title: Chunking

items.title: Spaced reviews for whole topics too
items.lead: Not everything needs a flashcard. Reviewing a whole topic by blank-page recall on day 1, 3, 7, 14 and 30 covers understanding as well as facts.

sections.title: Planning and organisation across a term

items.title: The lifecycle of one lesson, lecture or chapter
items.lead: Every unit of new material (a lecture, a school lesson, a textbook chapter, a week of a language course, a module of an online course) goes through the same…

items.title: Semester map
items.lead: At the start, list every course, exam date and assessment in one calendar. Count back from each exam.

items.title: Weekly plan
items.lead: Once a week (for example Sunday, about 20 minutes), look at the week's lessons, due reviews and deadlines. Block study time in the calendar like appointments.

items.title: Daily plan
items.lead: Spend about 5 minutes picking 1 to 3 must-do tasks for the day. Everything else is a bonus.

items.title: Time blocking
items.lead: Fixed study blocks at the same times each day turn studying into a routine rather than a daily decision.

items.title: Plan reviews before new material
items.lead: Reviews first each day, then new content. Skipping reviews is how backlogs start.

items.title: A catch-up rule
items.lead: If you fall behind, do not try to do everything. Do today's lessons first, then work the backlog in small chunks, highest-yield first.

items.title: Buffer days
items.lead: Leave one lighter day per week for catch-up and rest.

items.title: Single capture system
items.lead: Use one place for every task and deadline (a planner, a to-do app or a paper notebook). Nothing stays only in your head.

items.title: Weekly review
items.lead: Spend about 15 minutes on what got done, what slipped and what to change. This is where you adjust the method.

items.title: Support
items.lead: Get assessed and supportedIf ADHD is suspected or diagnosed, a doctor can discuss treatment, and school or university disability services, or your employer,…

items.title: Test yourself often, in low-stakes ways
items.lead: Frequent practice makes the real exam feel familiar.

items.title: Worry dump
items.lead: Spend 5 to 10 minutes writing down your worries before studying or before an exam. It frees up working memory.

items.title: Define a stopping point
items.lead: Anxious students often never feel "done". Decide in advance what a finished day looks like, and stop when you reach it.

items.title: Productive struggle vs panic
items.lead: Struggling to recall is normal and useful. Panic is a signal to pause, breathe and shrink the task.

items.title: Breathing
items.lead: A slow exhale, or two inhales through the nose and one long exhale (the physiological sigh), calms the body within a minute.

items.title: Reframe stress
items.lead: Telling yourself that a racing heart is your body getting ready to perform helps more than trying to calm down.

items.title: Self-compassion over perfectionism
items.lead: Talk to yourself the way you would talk to a friend. A missed day is data, not a failure.

items.title: Compare less
items.lead: Students in competitive programmes (medicine, law, engineering, music conservatoires, top schools) often compare hours, grades and resources. Track your own…

items.title: Sleep 7 to 9 hours
items.lead: Memory is consolidated during sleep. All-nighters lower exam performance.

items.title: Exercise
items.lead: Even a 20-minute walk improves mood, focus and sleep.

items.title: Food, caffeine and screens
items.lead: Regular meals, caffeine before early afternoon, and screens off before bed.

items.title: Protected time off
items.lead: At least one half-day per week without study. Rest is part of the plan.

items.title: Ask for help early
items.lead: University counselling, a doctor (GP), or student wellbeing services. Burnout and anxiety are common in demanding courses and are treatable.

items.title: Choose your own methods
items.lead: Experiment and keep what you like. Ownership of the method is itself motivating.

items.title: Make progress visible
items.lead: Question-bank percentages rising, a topic moving from "new" to "solid", a growing done list.

items.title: Gamify it
items.lead: Beat your own recall score, keep a forgiving streak (for example 5 of 7 days counts), earn points for sessions, race a friend through a question set.

items.title: Use fresh starts and forgive missed days
items.lead: When you fall off the plan, restart from the next natural landmark (a Monday, a new month, the start of a new topic) instead of waiting to "catch up" first.

items.title: Curiosity first
items.lead: Start a topic with a mystery: a puzzling case, a strange result, a "why does this happen?".

items.title: Connect it to your future use
items.lead: Ask "when would I actually need this?". For future patients, clients, a code base, a conversation in the language you are learning, a court case. Practical…

items.title: Variety
items.lead: Rotate places (library, café, home), methods and formats to keep things fresh.

items.title: Study socially
items.lead: Study groups, quizzing friends, teaching younger students, online study rooms.

items.title: Small wins and rewards
items.lead: Celebrate finished blocks, not just finished exams.

items.title: Identity, not willpower
items.lead: "I'm someone who reviews every day" lasts longer than relying on motivation each morning. Habits do the heavy lifting.

items.title: Habit stacking
items.lead: Attach study to something you already do (coffee, then flashcards).

items.title: Rest without guilt
items.lead: Planned breaks and days off prevent the burnout that kills motivation.

items.title: Revisit your why
items.lead: Write down why you chose this subject and read it during hard weeks.

items.title: Make it beautiful, a bit
items.lead: A good desk, a nice notebook, music without lyrics or a focus playlist, as long as it doesn't become the task itself.

items.title: Start practice questions early
items.lead: Start from the first weeks of the term, not the last two.

items.title: Past papers and question banks
items.lead: These are the best predictor of exam content. Notice what kinds of questions keep coming up.

items.title: Simulate the exam
items.lead: Use the same time limit, no notes, and the same time of day if possible. Do at least one full mock.

items.title: Error log
items.lead: For every wrong answer, note the topic, why you got it wrong (did not know it, misread the question, confused it with something else, ran out of time) and the…

items.title: Weak topics first
items.lead: Use question-bank statistics or your error log to choose what to review.

items.title: Interleave in the final weeks
items.lead: Mix courses and topics, the way the exam will.

items.title: Know the format
items.lead: Every exam format needs its own practice: multiple-choice questions (MCQs), short answers, essays, problem sets, oral exams, practical exams and speaking tests.

items.title: No new resources in the last week
items.lead: Stick to what you know.

items.title: Protect sleep before the exam
items.lead: Sleep matters more than one more late-night session.

items.title: Calm exam-day nerves
items.lead: Some nervousness helps; too much blocks memory. A few simple routines keep it in the helpful range.

items.title: During the exam
items.lead: Read each question carefully and know what it is asking before you answer, move on from hard questions and come back at the end.

items.title: After the exam
items.lead: Note what surprised you and adjust your method for the next block.

sections.title: Myths and low-yield habits to drop

items.title: Re-reading notes many times
items.lead: Re-reading builds familiarity, not recall. Read once, then test yourself.

items.title: Highlighting large parts of text
items.lead: Highlighting is passive, and when half the page is yellow, everything looks important. Highlight little, then turn highlights into questions.

items.title: Learning styles ("I'm a visual learner")
items.lead: Matching teaching to a preferred style has not been shown to improve learning. Use whatever format fits the content.

items.title: Long marathon sessions
items.lead: Attention and memory drop after long unbroken blocks. Use shorter, spaced blocks with breaks.

items.title: Rewriting notes neatly
items.lead: Rewriting takes hours and is mostly copying. Summarise from memory instead.

items.title: Watching videos passively
items.lead: Videos feel like learning, but little sticks. Pause and recall after each section.

items.title: Multitasking with phone and messages
items.lead: Each switch costs focus and time. Put the phone in another room during focus blocks.

items.title: All-nighters before exams
items.lead: Sleep loss hurts memory and reasoning. Spread the work and sleep before exams.

items.title: More resources means more learning
items.lead: Extra resources spread attention thin. Pick one spine and add targeted extras.

items.title: Hours studied as the measure of progress
items.lead: Hours don't equal learning. Measure recall, question scores and topics mastered.
